pos: n. (Laurence Chaderton, c. 1536–1640, first Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, Puritan preacher, and King James translator)
etymology: Latin Laurentius, of Laurentum, crowned with laurel; English Chaderton, a Lancashire place-name.
biblical_def: Laurence Chaderton was born to a Roman Catholic family in Lancashire and disinherited by his father when he embraced the Reformed faith at Cambridge. He became a fellow of Christ's College and for some fifty years preached the Sunday afternoon lecture at St Clement's church in Cambridge, where generations of students heard plain, doctrinal, practical preaching of the kind William Perkins would make famous. In 1584 Sir Walter Mildmay founded Emmanuel College as a seminary for a godly preaching ministry and made Chaderton its first Master; he held the office until 1622, and Emmanuel became the nursery of the Puritan ministry, sending out John Cotton, Thomas Hooker, Thomas Shepard, and many who would found New England. At the Hampton Court Conference in 1604 Chaderton was one of the four Puritan representatives, and he served in the First Cambridge Company of the translators of the King James Bible. He was moderate in temper, conforming where conscience allowed and steadily pressing for a learned, preaching ministry. He lived to be over a hundred. His aim for every Emmanuel man was Paul's: “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lecturer as one who reads or pronounces lectures, especially an assistant preacher in a parish church.
webster_full: LEC'TURER, n. One who reads or pronounces lectures; a professor or an instructor who delivers formal discourses for the instruction of others; a preacher in a church, hired by the parish to assist the rector.
COL'LEGE, n. A society of men, invested with certain powers and rights, performing certain duties, or engaged in some common employment or pursuit.
TRANSLA'TOR, n. One that renders into another language.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Act 6:4
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Emmanuel's first Master, who gave England and New England a preaching ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Chaderton served is under quiet pressure wherever the ministry is reimagined as leadership, counselling, or management: that God's ordinary means of saving sinners is the preaching of His Word. “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Emmanuel was founded to supply that means, and the apostles' division of labour was its charter: “we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4).

The honest caveat is Chaderton's conformity, which some of his own students thought too ready. The principle to recover is that a church which wants a reformed ministry must build the schools that form one, and honour the men who “labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17).

roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, divide rightly; 2 Timothy 2:15.

“faith cometh by hearing” (Rom 10:17) — why a college for preachers.
“to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4) — fifty years at St Clement's.

pos: n. (the conference of Puritan ministers that met around Dedham in Essex from 1582 to 1589, whose minutes survive)
etymology: Dedham, a village on the Stour in Essex; Latin classis, a division, class.
biblical_def: The Dedham Classis was a voluntary conference of some twenty Puritan ministers in the Stour valley of north Essex and south Suffolk, who met monthly from October 1582 until the spring of 1589. Its members were beneficed clergy and lecturers of the Church of England, among them Edmund Chapman, the lecturer at Dedham, and Richard Parker of Dedham. They opened each meeting with prayer, heard one of their number expound a text, and then took up questions laid before them: how to deal with an unworthy communicant, whether a minister might wear the surplice, how to secure the Sabbath against fairs and alehouses, how to provide preaching for parishes without it, and how far the presbyterian discipline set out in Walter Travers's Book of Discipline might be practised within the established church. Their minute book, kept by the secretary and published in 1905, is the fullest surviving record of the Elizabethan classical movement, by which Puritan ministers tried to build a presbyterian church inside the episcopal one. The conference ended when Archbishop Whitgift's campaign against the movement brought its leaders before the courts. Its spirit was the prophet's: “they that feared the LORD spake often one to another” (Mal 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a classis as a convention or assembly, and a conference as a meeting for consultation.
webster_full: CLAS'SIS, n. Order; sort; body. In some churches, an ecclesiastical body or judicatory.
CON'FERENCE, n. The act of conversing on a serious subject; a meeting of the ministers of a church for consultation.
MIN'UTE, n. A short sketch of any agreement or other subject, taken in writing; a note to preserve the memory of any thing.
scriptures: Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
corruption_summary: A monthly meeting of Essex ministers who practised presbyterian counsel inside the Elizabethan church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Dedham minutes show the Puritan ministry at its most ordinary and its most admirable: men meeting to sharpen one another in exposition and to seek counsel on hard cases of conscience. “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17). The classis was the pattern of the apostolic assembly, where “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6).

The honest caveat is the ambiguity of their position, holding office under bishops while practising a discipline that denied the bishops' authority. The principle to recover is that ministers need one another's counsel, and that a church without regular assemblies of its elders leaves every pastor to judge alone: “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14).

usage: “spake often one to another” (Mal 3:16) — the monthly conference.
“Iron sharpeneth iron” (Pro 27:17) — mutual exposition.
“in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — cases of conscience in common.

pos: n. (the dispute over clerical vestments in the Elizabethan church, at its height in 1563–1567)
etymology: Latin vestiarium, a wardrobe, from vestis, a garment; controversia, a turning against.
biblical_def: The Vestiarian Controversy was the first open conflict between the Puritans and the Elizabethan bishops, and it was about clothes. The quarrel had a precedent in 1550, when John Hooper refused to be consecrated bishop of Gloucester in the vestments of the old rite. Under Elizabeth many returning exiles, who had worshipped in Zurich, Frankfurt, and Geneva, objected to the surplice in parish worship and the cope at the communion, which the queen required by the Act of Uniformity. They argued that garments associated with the mass taught the people that the minister was still a sacrificing priest, and that the church should not impose ceremonies Scripture did not command. In 1565 Thomas Sampson and Laurence Humphrey, heads of two Oxford colleges, refused to conform, and Sampson was deprived. In 1566 Archbishop Matthew Parker issued his Advertisements requiring the surplice, and thirty-seven London ministers who refused were suspended. Bullinger and other continental Reformers counselled the objectors to conform for the sake of the pulpit, holding vestments indifferent; some did, and in 1567 a group of Londoners who would not was arrested meeting separately at Plumbers' Hall. The objectors appealed to Paul: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vestment as a garment, especially some part of clerical dress, and a surplice as a white garment worn by clergymen.
webster_full: VEST'MENT, n. A garment; some part of clothing or dress; especially, some part of outer clothing.
SUR'PLICE, n. A white garment worn by clergymen of some denominations over their other dress, in their ministrations.
ADIAPH'OROUS, a. Indifferent; neutral; things neither commanded nor forbidden.
scriptures: Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: The surplice quarrel: whether the church may impose ceremonies Scripture does not command.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The controversy is easily mocked as a fight over linen. It was a fight over the regulative principle. If the church may impose garments that carry a doctrinal meaning Scripture rejects, it may impose any ceremony it likes, and the worship of God is governed by the church's will and not by His Word. Christ's rebuke applies: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9).

The honest caveat is that the objectors' friends abroad thought the surplice a thing indifferent and the cost of refusing it too high, and that Paul's rule of order, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40), does leave the church some discretion. The principle to recover is that what is truly indifferent may not be made a condition of ministry, and that a conscience bound by Scripture is not to be forced, for “whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23).
usage: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty” (Gal 5:1) — the objectors' appeal.
“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — imposed ceremonies.
“whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23) — the bound conscience.

pos: n. (the Puritan manifesto of 1572 by John Field and Thomas Wilcox calling for a presbyterian reformation of the Church of England)
etymology: Latin admonitio, a reminding, warning; Old French parlement, a speaking.
biblical_def: The Admonition to Parliament was published anonymously in June 1572, after Parliament had failed to pass bills for further reform of the church. Its authors were two young London ministers, John Field and Thomas Wilcox, who were imprisoned for a year in Newgate for it. The Admonition argued that the Church of England was so far from being reformed according to the Word of God that it had not yet come to the outward face of a true church: it attacked the Prayer Book as culled out of the popish mass-book, the vestments, the government of the church by archbishops, bishops, and their courts, and the absence of a preaching ministry in thousands of parishes; and it set out, from the New Testament, a church governed by ministers, elders, and deacons chosen by the congregation and joined in assemblies. A Second Admonition followed later that year. John Whitgift, then Master of Trinity College, Cambridge, answered it, Thomas Cartwright replied to Whitgift, and the exchange that followed became the classic debate of the Elizabethan church over whether Scripture prescribes the government of the church. The Admonition's premise was Paul's: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction” (2Ti 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines admonition as gentle reproof, counseling against a fault, and a manifesto as a public declaration.
webster_full: ADMONI'TION, n. Gentle or friendly reproof; counseling against a fault; instruction in duties; caution; direction.
PAR'LIAMENT, n. In Great Britain, the grand assembly of the three estates, the lords spiritual, lords temporal, and commons.
MANIFES'TO, n. A public declaration, usually of a prince or sovereign, showing his intentions.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Heb 8:5

Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
corruption_summary: The first Puritan manifesto for a church governed by Scripture rather than by bishops' courts.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Admonition's central claim is the one Whitgift denied and Hooker would later answer at length: that Scripture gives a pattern for the government of the church, as Moses received one for the tabernacle, “See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5). Paul left Titus to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5), not to appoint diocesan lords.

The honest caveat is the Admonition's tone, which was harsh enough to embarrass its own friends; Cartwright and others regretted its bitterness even as they defended its substance. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Scripture for the church's order as well as its doctrine, under the one Master of Mat 23:8, “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).

“according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5) — the case for a scriptural polity.
“ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — the government the Admonition asked for.

pos: n. (Walter Travers, c. 1548–1635, Puritan divine, author of the Book of Discipline, and Richard Hooker's adversary at the Temple)
etymology: Germanic Walter, ruler of the army; Norman French Travers, a crossing.
biblical_def: Walter Travers was a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, who left England after quarrelling with Whitgift and visited Geneva, where he came to know Beza. In 1574 he published in Latin A Full and Plain Declaration of Ecclesiastical Discipline, translated into English by Thomas Cartwright, the most learned statement of the presbyterian case in Elizabethan England. Unwilling to accept episcopal orders, he was ordained by the presbytery of the English congregation at Antwerp in 1578. In 1581 he became afternoon lecturer at the Temple Church in London, and when Richard Hooker was made its master in 1585 the two preached against one another week by week, so that, as Thomas Fuller later put it, the forenoon sermon spoke Canterbury and the afternoon Geneva. Travers charged Hooker with teaching that Roman Catholics might be saved despite their errors and with defective views of justification. Whitgift silenced Travers in 1586 on the ground that his ordination was not valid in England. He drafted the Book of Discipline used by the classical movement, and from 1594 to 1598 was provost of Trinity College, Dublin, where young James Ussher was among his students. His conviction was the apostolic order: the elders “that rule well be counted worthy of double honour” (1Ti 5:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discipline in the church as the execution of the laws by which the church is governed.
webster_full: DIS'CIPLINE, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, the execution of the laws by which the church is governed, and infliction of the penalties enjoined against offenders.
PROV'OST, n. A person who is appointed to superintend or preside over something; the head of a college.
ORDINA'TION, n. The act of conferring holy orders, or of setting apart for the gospel ministry.
scriptures: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Gal 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
corruption_summary: The presbyterian theorist silenced because his ordination came from a presbytery, not a bishop.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The ground on which Travers was silenced is itself the corruption: that ordination by a presbytery of Reformed ministers, the ordination of every Reformed church on the Continent, was no ordination in England. Paul told the Ephesian elders that the Holy Ghost had made them overseers (Act 20:28), and called the same men elders and bishops; a church that would not own the orders of Geneva and Antwerp had made its bishops the measure of the ministry.

His contest with Hooker is a second lesson. It is easy now to admire Hooker's prose and dismiss Travers as a narrow controversialist. But on justification and on the necessity of confessing Christ alone, Travers stood where the Reformers stood, and his public correction of a colleague had apostolic warrant: “I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed” (Gal 2:11).
roots_lines: Greek proistemi (G4291) — to stand before, rule; 1 Timothy 5:17.
usage: “the elders that rule well” (1Ti 5:17) — the ruling eldership he defended.
“I withstood him to the face” (Gal 2:11) — the afternoon lectures at the Temple.
“the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28) — elders and bishops one office.

pos: n. (the seven satirical pamphlets against the English bishops published on a secret press in 1588–1589 under the name Martin Marprelate)
etymology: English mar, to spoil, and prelate, a bishop: Martin the spoiler of prelates.
biblical_def: The Marprelate Tracts were seven pamphlets published between October 1588 and September 1589 by an anonymous writer calling himself Martin Marprelate, Gentleman. Printed first by Robert Waldegrave on a secret press that was moved from house to house in the Midlands to escape the authorities, they ridiculed the bishops of the Church of England, and especially Archbishop Whitgift and Bishop John Aylmer of London, in a style of rough comic abuse that England had never seen in religious controversy. They also made a serious case: that the bishops' government was unscriptural, that their courts persecuted godly preachers, and that the people were starved of the Word. The tracts were wildly popular and wholly disastrous for the cause they served. The government seized the press at Manchester in August 1589, hired its own pamphleteers to answer Martin in kind, and used the scandal to crush the classical movement; Richard Bancroft's sermon at Paul's Cross that year attacked the presbyterian platform root and branch. The author was probably Job Throkmorton, a Warwickshire gentleman; John Penry, who helped run the press, was hanged in 1593. The tracts stand under Paul's rule: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth” (Eph 4:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines satire as a discourse in which wickedness or folly is exposed with severity, and a prelate as an ecclesiastic of superior order.
webster_full: SAT'IRE, n. A discourse or poem in which wickedness or folly is exposed with severity.
PREL'ATE, n. An ecclesiastic of a higher order, as an archbishop, bishop or patriarch; a dignitary of the church.
PAMPH'LET, n. A small book consisting of a sheet of paper, or of sheets stitched together but not bound.
scriptures: Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Pro 26:5
Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit.
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
corruption_summary: Satire against the bishops that delighted the public and ruined the Puritan cause.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Martin's defenders can cite Pro 26:5, “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit” (Pro 26:5), and his grievances were real. But the verse before it says the opposite, and the tracts show why both are in Scripture: mockery that exposes pride once becomes, repeated, the very folly it mocks. The serious Puritans of the day were appalled, and they paid for Martin's jokes with their pulpits.

The lesson applies with force to every age of pamphlets, and none more than one of instant publication. The principle to recover is Christ's example under provocation, “when he was reviled, reviled not again” (1Pe 2:23), and the proverb's plain wisdom, “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger” (Pro 15:1).

roots_lines: Greek loidoreo (G3058) — to revile, rail at; 1 Peter 2:23.

“Answer a fool according to his folly” (Pro 26:5) — his defenders' text.
“when he was reviled, reviled not again” (1Pe 2:23) — the better way.

pos: n. (the petition presented to James I in April 1603 by Puritan ministers claiming to number a thousand, asking for reform of the Church of England)
etymology: Latin millenarius, containing a thousand; petitio, a request.
biblical_def: The Millenary Petition was handed to James VI of Scotland as he travelled south in April 1603 to take the English throne as James I. Its framers described themselves as more than a thousand ministers of the Church of England, groaning under a common burden of human rites and ceremonies, and they asked, not for the overthrow of the bishops, but for moderate reform of particular abuses. In the services, they asked that the sign of the cross in baptism, the questions put to infants, confirmation, the ring in marriage, bowing at the name of Jesus, and the reading of the Apocrypha in church be taken away, and that the cap and surplice not be urged. In the ministry, they asked that none be admitted but able and sufficient men who would preach diligently, especially on the Lord's Day, and that non-residence and the holding of several livings be ended. In discipline, they asked that excommunication not be pronounced by lay officials for trifles. Because James had been raised in the Church of Scotland, the petitioners hoped for a sympathetic king. Their petition led to the Hampton Court Conference of January 1604, where they gained little except the new translation of the Bible. Their chief request was Paul's charge to Timothy: “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a petition as a formal request or supplication, particularly to a sovereign or legislature.
webster_full: PETI'TION, n. A formal request or supplication, from an inferior to a superior, either to a single person clothed with power, or to a legislative or other body.
NON-RES'IDENCE, n. Failure or neglect of residing at the place where one is stationed, or where official duties require one to reside.
CER'EMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion.
scriptures: Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Rev 1:10
I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and heard behind me a great voice, as of a trumpet,
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
corruption_summary: A modest Puritan request for a preaching ministry and the removal of unscriptural ceremonies.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Petition is a reminder that the Puritans were not, in the main, revolutionaries. Their requests were modest and their reasons scriptural: ceremonies that Scripture does not command should not be urged on the conscience, for in such things men “worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9), and parishes should have ministers who preach.

The principle to recover is the priority of the preached Word in the life of the church. A thousand ministers asked a king for preachers on the Lord's Day, the day John was “in the Spirit on the Lord's day” (Rev 1:10). James gave them a Bible instead, and the gift was providential; but a Bible unread in a parish without a preacher was exactly their complaint.

roots_lines: Greek prosecho (G4337) — to attend to, give heed; 1 Timothy 4:13.
Greek kuriakos (G2960) — belonging to the Lord; Revelation 1:10.

“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — the ceremonies they asked to be spared.
“on the Lord's day” (Rev 1:10) — the day they wanted preached.

pos: n. (the royal Declaration of Sports of James I, 1618, reissued by Charles I in 1633, permitting recreations on the Lord's Day)
etymology: Old English boc, book; Middle English disport, recreation, from Old French desporter, to divert.
biblical_def: The Book of Sports was a royal declaration first issued by James I for Lancashire in 1617, after a quarrel between Puritan magistrates and Catholic gentry over Sunday games, and extended to the whole kingdom in 1618. It declared that after divine service on the Lord's Day the people should not be hindered from lawful recreations such as dancing, archery, leaping, vaulting, May games, Whitsun ales, morris dances, and the setting up of maypoles, though bear-baiting, bull-baiting, interludes, and bowling remained forbidden. James had meant to have it read in every church but withdrew the order. In 1633 Charles I, at the urging of William Laud, reissued the declaration and required the clergy to read it from their pulpits. Many Puritan ministers refused; some read it and then read the fourth commandment after it; a number were suspended or deprived, and the controversy did much to drive godly men toward emigration and toward Parliament. In 1643 Parliament ordered the book publicly burned by the hangman. The ministers who would not read it stood on the commandment, “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8), and on Isaiah's description of the day kept “not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure” (Isa 58:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sport as play, diversion, or that which diverts and makes mirth, and the sabbath as the day of rest.
webster_full: SPORT, n. That which diverts and makes mirth; pastime; diversion; play.
SAB'BATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest; among christians, the first day of the week, in commemoration of the resurrection of Christ.
DECLARA'TION, n. A proclamation or affirmation; publication.
scriptures: Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:
Rev 1:10
I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and heard behind me a great voice, as of a trumpet,
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: A royal order to the clergy to proclaim Sunday sports from the pulpit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Book of Sports was a deliberate assault on the Puritan doctrine of the Lord's Day, and in 1633 an assault on the consciences of ministers, who were ordered to announce from the pulpit a permission they believed the fourth commandment forbade. When the crown commands a minister to preach against God's law, the answer is the apostles': “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

The corruption is not dead because the declaration was burned. The modern Christian Sunday, given over to sport and commerce after a morning service, is the Book of Sports without the king. The principle to recover is that the Lord's Day belongs to the Lord, the day John was “in the Spirit on the Lord's day” (Rev 1:10), and is to be kept as a delight in Him rather than in our own pleasure.

roots_lines: Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to keep holy, sanctify; Exodus 20:8.
Greek kuriakos (G2960) — belonging to the Lord; Revelation 1:10.

“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the ministers who would not read it.

pos: n. (the London petition of December 1640 asking the Long Parliament to abolish episcopacy entirely)
etymology: Old Norse rot, root; Old French branche, branch; Latin petitio, a request.
biblical_def: The Root and Branch Petition was presented to the House of Commons on 11 December 1640, a month after the Long Parliament first met, by Alderman Isaac Pennington and a crowd of London citizens, bearing some fifteen thousand signatures. It asked that the government of the church by archbishops, bishops, deans, and archdeacons, with all its dependencies, roots and branches, be abolished, and it listed twenty-eight grievances against the bishops: the silencing of godly ministers, the suppression of lectures, the Book of Sports, the Laudian altar policy and bowing toward the communion table, the persecution of conscience in the High Commission, the encouragement of Arminian and popish doctrine, and the corruption of the ecclesiastical courts. Parliament debated the petition and a Root and Branch Bill in 1641; the moderates who wished to reform episcopacy rather than end it resisted, and the division between them became one of the lines along which the nation split into civil war. Episcopacy was finally abolished by ordinance in 1646. The phrase came from the prophet, who foretold a day when the proud would be burned up so that “it shall leave them neither root nor branch” (Mal 4:1), and from Christ: “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Mat 15:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines episcopacy as government of the church by bishops, and to eradicate as to pull up by the roots.
webster_full: EPIS'COPACY, n. Government of the church by bishops; that form of ecclesiastical government in which diocesan bishops are established, as distinct from and superior to priests or presbyters.
ERAD'ICATE, v.t. To pull up the roots, or by the roots; to destroy any thing that grows.
GRIEV'ANCE, n. That which causes grief or uneasiness; that which burdens, oppresses or injures.
scriptures: But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.
Mal 4:1

For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: London's demand that the bishops' government be abolished, not merely reformed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Petition's premise was that diocesan episcopacy is not a plant of the Father's planting, and that a government which had become an instrument of persecution could not be pruned into health. Peter's charge to elders forbids the very thing the grievances described, ruling “as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3), and Paul names the elders themselves the overseers of the flock (Act 20:28).

The honest caveat is that the abolition of episcopacy came by Parliament and war rather than by the church's own assemblies, and that what replaced it was never fully settled before the Restoration undid it. The principle to recover is that reformation of the church's government must be by Scripture and by the church, and that a root-and-branch reform carried by political force is carried away by the next political force.
roots_summary: Greek ekrizoo (G1610), to root up; phuteia (G5451), a plant; Hebrew shoresh (H8328), root.
roots_lines: Greek ekrizoo (G1610) — to root out, pluck up by the roots; Matthew 15:13.
usage: “shall be rooted up” (Mat 15:13) — the petitioners' text.
“neither root nor branch” (Mal 4:1) — the source of the phrase.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3) — the charge against the bishops.

pos: n. (the five Independent divines at the Westminster Assembly — Goodwin, Nye, Simpson, Burroughs, and Bridge — authors of An Apologeticall Narration, 1644)
etymology: Latin dissentire, to differ in feeling; Old English brothru, brethren.
biblical_def: The Dissenting Brethren were the five Congregational ministers who sat in the Westminster Assembly as the leading voices of the Independent minority: Thomas Goodwin, Philip Nye, Sidrach Simpson, Jeremiah Burroughs, and William Bridge. Four of them had spent the 1630s in exile in the Netherlands, pastoring English congregations at Arnhem and Rotterdam, and had there worked out a moderate Congregationalism. In January 1644 they published An Apologeticall Narration, addressed to Parliament, in which they professed full agreement with the Reformed churches in doctrine, distanced themselves from the Brownists and Separatists, and argued that each particular congregation has the whole power of government within itself, that synods may counsel and admonish but not exercise authority over congregations, and that they should be allowed liberty to gather churches on that pattern. The Scottish commissioners and the Presbyterian majority of the Assembly answered them at length, and the long debate over church government in 1644–46 set Presbyterian against Independent in the Assembly, the City, and the army. The Dissenting Brethren agreed with the Assembly's doctrine, and in 1658 their party produced the Savoy Declaration, a lightly revised Westminster Confession with a Congregational platform. They appealed to the liberty of Paul's counsel: “if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you” (Phi 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dissenter as one who separates from the established church, and independency as the system of the Independents.
webster_full: DISSENT'ER, n. One who dissents; one who separates from the service and worship of any established church.
INDEPEND'ENT, n. One who maintains that every congregation of christians is a complete church, subject to no superior authority.
NARRA'TION, n. Recital; rehearsal; relation of facts or events in the order in which they happened.
scriptures: Phi 3:15
Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Act 15:2

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.

Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:
corruption_summary: Five Independents who agreed with Westminster's doctrine and dissented from its presbytery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dispute between the Dissenting Brethren and the Presbyterians was a disagreement between brethren who held the same confession, and both sides argued from the same texts. The Independents stressed Christ's word, “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17), as placing discipline in the congregation; the Presbyterians answered with Antioch's appeal to Jerusalem, where Paul and Barnabas were sent “unto the apostles and elders about this question” (Act 15:2).

The principle to recover is the one the Brethren's own career illustrates: that differences of polity among the orthodox are real and worth arguing, but do not unchurch those who hold the same faith. Their insistence that they agreed with the Assembly's doctrine, later proven by Savoy, is a model for confessional churches that differ on government.
roots_summary: Greek phroneo (G5426), to be minded; ekklesia (G1577), church; zetema (G2213), question.
roots_lines: Greek phroneo (G5426) — to think, be minded; Philippians 3:15.
usage: “if in any thing ye be otherwise minded” (Phi 3:15) — the Brethren's plea for liberty.
“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — the Independent text.
“unto the apostles and elders about this question” (Act 15:2) — the Presbyterian reply.
